editorial.headline: Islamic Primary Education: A Clearer Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: An Indonesian primary Islamic education activity that is nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, with address verification still required.
editorial.body:
This activity covers primary-level Islamic education for learners aged seven to twelve, alongside related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is Islamic scholarship: Qur’anic studies, hadith, fiqh, Islamic history and Arabic are all within scope. Yet the definition is not narrow or devotional-only. It also includes the teaching of general knowledge and practical skills, placing religious learning within a broader primary education setting.

The scope names several established forms through which that education may be delivered: madrasah ibtidaiyah, ula-level muadalah education, formal diniyah ula education, and ula-level pesantren teaching centred on the study of classical Islamic texts. It also includes equivalency education at salafiyah Islamic boarding schools at the same level. In other words, this is an activity defined by a distinct primary educational stage and a recognisably Islamic curriculum, while retaining general learning as part of the educational offer. The slim record does not list business-scale categories open to this activity.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is marked open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the national entry permits full foreign ownership; there is no lower foreign-share cap stated in the record. The relevant national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the activity at the national level, the classification presents an open route rather than a restricted one.

Bali calls for a closer reading, without warranting pessimism. This activity is marked `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK` and is classified as medium-high or high risk, so it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the province; this entry sits outside that bar. For Bali, the decisive point is that the activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium, although the address still needs verification. The record’s instruction to verify by address should therefore be treated as part of the registration check, not as evidence of a Bali-wide prohibition.
